title: 40,000 Ottomans Lay Siege to Malta — and Lose to a Few Hundred Knights
dek: In 1565 an Ottoman fleet of 180 ships and 40,000 men besieged Malta, defended by roughly 500 knights and a few thousand Maltese. Fort St Elmo held out for a month before falling, but the delay lasted until Sicilian reinforcements landed in September and the Ottomans withdrew.
why: This is on-location siege narrative — vivid but light on analysis. If you want the mechanics of why Malta held, the middle and later sections on scorched earth and disinformation are the most valuable.
who: Listeners interested in Mediterranean history, military history and siege warfare; anyone who wants concrete images of how 16th-century gunpowder-era attack and defence actually worked.
skip: The show promo at 0:00-1:00 and the subscription ad after 28:26 can be skipped.

points.h: Malta's value is its position, not its resources
points.body: Malta sits almost exactly in the middle of the Mediterranean: 80 km north of Sicily, hard against North Africa to the south, and roughly equidistant from Gibraltar and the Suez Canal. Whoever controls Malta controls the trade routes. The Grand Harbour where Valletta now stands is a rare natural deep-water port, safe to anchor in no matter which way the wind blows. The Knights did not initially want Malta — there was no existing fortress and no resources — and only took it because the first Grand Master insisted on having a foothold.

points.h: What the Knights brought was the Italian bastion
points.body: The Knights brought Italian-style military architecture (Traccia Italiana) to Malta: no longer the tall medieval castle but low, sloped, outward-projecting bastions with thick walls packed with earth to absorb the impact of gunpowder artillery. Fort St Angelo got the first bastion. By 1552 the Knights had realised how dangerous their position was, and the Grand Master Domades pushed hard to build fortifications. An underwater iron chain was also strung between St Angelo and Fort St Michael at Senglea, serving much like a WWII anti-submarine net to block ships.

points.h: The defenders were waiting for a fleet on the horizon
points.body: On 18 May 1565 the garrison of Fort St Elmo saw a vast fleet closing on the horizon, signalled at once, and the whole island went to war footing. The defenders numbered about 10,000 in total, including knights, Maltese civilians and mercenaries hired from Italy. This was not a war you could surrender in: the losers would be killed or sold as slaves, so for many it was a fight to the death. The Ottomans, for their part, arrived thinking they would take the place in a few days and move on to the next target, and set their first objective on Fort St Elmo.

points.h: Fort St Elmo held only a month, but it held the Ottomans
points.body: The Ottoman fleet of about 190 ships and an estimated 35,000 soldiers arrived at the Grand Harbour and did not strike directly at the Knights' headquarters at St Angelo, but first attacked Fort St Elmo, which guarded the entrances to both harbours. Fire opened on 27 May, with hundreds of guns bombarding almost without pause and reducing the walls to rubble; every night the Knights patched the breaches, hauled ammunition and treated the wounded, then fought again the next day. Fort St Elmo had been thrown up in only about six months and was not well built, so the Ottomans found it relatively easy to scale and dismantle. The Grand Master's strategy was simply to keep the Ottomans attacking and keep bleeding them. By the night of 22 June the fort was a ruin, and the surviving defenders said Mass in the chapel, preparing not for victory but for death. At noon on 23 June the last knights died fighting and Fort St Elmo fell.

points.h: Both sides used corpses to send a message
points.body: This was a war with no room for surrender. After the last defenders of Fort St Elmo were killed, the Ottomans cut off their heads and lashed the bodies to rafts in the shape of a cross, casting them into the sea as a warning to the Grand Master of what was coming. The Grand Master is said to have fired the Ottomans' own heads back from the guns of St Angelo in reply. On 15 July the Ottomans tried to attack Senglea, but there was a small battery at sea level below St Angelo that the Ottomans had not spotted, and when it opened fire they were caught completely off guard; nearly all the attacking boats were sunk.

points.h: Scorched earth broke the Ottomans first
points.body: By July the Knights' supplies were still adequate; it was the Ottomans who had the problem. The Knights and the Maltese waged scorched earth, burning everything as they withdrew, so the Ottomans could find no food at all. It was the height of summer, the heat was punishing, and Ottoman morale began to sink into panic. The Grand Master's tactic was to wear down the enemy's manpower and will until they gave up on their own. One Ottoman leader is said to have remarked that if St Elmo had taken this long, what would St Angelo cost them. Maltese civilians fought in large numbers too, including women who took part in nursing and in combat.

points.h: A tiny cavalry force scared off an Ottomans army on the brink of winning
points.body: In early August the Ottomans attacked both Birgu and Senglea at once, broke through the walls at one point, and fought a bloody close-quarters struggle in the streets that looked to be going their way. The Knights countered with a ruse: a commander at Mdina, the inland Maltese fortress city, sent out a very small force of Maltese cavalry that raided the Ottoman field hospital and supply camp. Rumour spread fast through the Ottoman army that a huge relief force had arrived. The Ottoman commander Mustafa Pasha broke off the assault, retreating on the edge of victory. By late August both sides were locked in a war of attrition, with disease, hunger and casualties mounting, and the Ottomans had lost experienced commanders such as Dragut.

points.h: The relief came, but the Ottoman Empire was not broken
points.body: On 7 September 1565, 8,000 Spanish, Italian and Sicilian troops dispatched by Don Garcia in the name of Philip II of Spain landed on Malta from Sicily and advanced on the exhausted Ottoman army. The Knights had been begging for help for weeks, and the relief was late but it came. The Ottomans formally surrendered. But Kirsty stresses that this did not weaken the Ottoman Empire's power or legitimacy — it endured as an empire for a long time afterwards, and today people tend to inflate the significance of this victory. After the siege the Knights immediately set about building the new city of Valletta and repairing Fort St Elmo; the Grand Master La Valette died before he saw the city finished.

So they had to build bastions that are strong, low, of course, and filled with earth, so that the impact of the gunpowder wouldn't be as intense.
